note:
Solomon succeeds David as king in spite of political turmoil and intrigue by Adonijah, Abiathar, Joab, and Shimei.

**1:1 old and advanced in years.** As 1 Kings begins, David is about seventy years old (2 Sam. 5:4; 1 Kin. 2:11).
Shunem is sixteen miles (26 km) southwest of the Sea of Chinneroth (Galilee), near Mount Gilboa (Josh. 19:18; 1 Sam. 28:4; 2 Kin. 4:8).

This underlines David’s frailty and suggests that he no longer has the physical strength to be king. Since David does not have sexual relations with Abishag, Adonijah’s later request to marry her (2:17) is not against the law of Deut. 22:30.

Probably the oldest living son of David (2 Sam. 3:2–5; 13:28; 18:14). As such, he may believe that he will succeed his father. However, Deut. 17 emphasizes that the king should be the one chosen by God. Adonijah, who strives to make himself king, is rejected by God (cf. Abimelech in Judg. 9).

**chariots and horsemen.** Like Absalom before him (2 Sam. 15:1), Adonijah signals his ambitions and positions himself to take the throne.

verse_quote: had never at any time displeased him.
note:
As in dealing with his other rebellious sons, David makes no attempt to either question or discipline Adonijah. But his patience and forgiveness seem only to invite further rebellion (2 Sam. 13:32, 39; 14:33; 18:5).

**very handsome.** Handsome features are an asset for someone aspiring to the throne (1 Sam. 9:2; 16:12; 2 Sam. 14:25, 26), but God looks at inward qualities (1 Sam. 13:14 note; 16:7).

Joab is the commander of the army of Israel and one of David’s longtime supporters (2 Sam. 2:13; 8:16; 18:2; 20:10, 23). His relationship with David has been strained by his harsh actions in putting down rebellions (2 Sam. 18:5; 19:5–8, 13; 1 Kin. 2:5, 6).

**Abiathar the priest.** Abiathar and Zadok are the two high priests appointed by David (1 Sam. 22:20–22; 2 Sam. 8:17 note).

Benaiah is the commander of the Cherethites and Pelethites, mercenary forces who have functioned in large measure as David’s royal guard (2 Sam. 8:18; 20:7; 23:20; 1 Chr. 18:17).

**Nathan the prophet.** The most prominent prophet during David’s reign (2 Sam. 7:1–17; 12:1–15).

**Shimei.** A different man from the one referred to in 2 Sam. 16:5–8; 1 Kin. 2:8, 36–46. Perhaps this person is “Shimei the son of Ela,” one of Solomon’s governors (4:18).

**mighty men.** See 2 Sam. 23:8–39.

Again, Adonijah follows the example of Absalom (1:5 and notes; cf. 2 Sam. 15:7–12). This activity appears to be a coronation sacrifice and banquet (1:41; cf. 1 Sam. 9:22–24; 2 Sam. 15:10–12).

**En-rogel.** This spring is located south of the city. Because of their importance to the city, springs are considered to be an appropriate place for such activity (cf. 2 Sam. 17:17).

Queen mothers can play an influential role in the affairs of state (2:19; 15:13; 2 Kin. 10:13). As Solomon’s mother, Bathsheba has a major interest in seeing that Adonijah is thwarted in his plans to become king.

verse_quote: save your own life and the life of your son.
note: Since contenders for the throne in the ancient Near East often sought to consolidate their positions by eliminating all potential rivals, Nathan’s advice conveys a sense of urgency (cf. 15:29; 2 Kin. 10:11; 11:1).

Nathan’s advice plays on the ambiguity and instability inherent during a coup attempt. Actually David is still king, but Nathan’s words underscore the fact that Adonijah has also publicly claimed this status (vv. 5, 9). By confirming Bathsheba’s concerns, Nathan underscores the gravity of the situation to the “very old” king (v. 15).

In Israel an oath taken in the Lord’s name constitutes a sacred obligation and, as such, is considered inviolable (Ex. 20:7; Lev. 19:12; Josh. 9:15, 18, 20; Judg. 11:30, 35; Eccl. 5:4–7). For the oath, see 1 Chr. 22:9, 10.

verse_quote: tell them who shall sit on the throne.
note: Only a public declaration that Solomon will succeed David as king will suffice to turn back Adonijah’s claim to the throne.

Nathan incisively attacks the issue. Either David has privately affirmed Adonijah as heir apparent (and hence Nathan, Zadok, and Benaiah have been shunned), or David has not done so (and hence Adonijah has rebelled against his father).

verse_quote: Solomon your son shall reign after me.
note: Solomon will be the offspring through whom God will fulfill His promise of establishing the throne of his kingdom forever (2 Sam. 7:12, 13).

Mules and donkeys are used as mounts of royalty (Judg. 10:4; 2 Sam. 13:29; 18:9; Zech. 9:9). David is therefore making a public declaration that Solomon is the heir. The triumphal entry of Christ may be a symbol of His kingship as the son of David (see Matt. 21:1–11).

**Gihon.** The Gihon spring, located about one-half mile (0.8 km) north of En-rogel (v. 9), is a major supply of water for Jerusalem in this era (2 Chr. 32:30; 33:14). Due to topography, En-rogel is not visible from Gihon; however, the two are within earshot (v. 41).

Priests (Ex. 28:41; 29:4–9; Lev. 4:3, 5, 16), kings (1 Sam. 2:10; 9:16; 10:1), and occasionally prophets (1 Kin. 19:16), were anointed in ancient Israel. The Hebrew for “anointed” became a technical term for the Lord’s anointed, usually with royal connotations. The title is usually transliterated “messiah.” The Gk. word for “anointed” is _christos_ (“Christ,” Matt. 1:17). Although Solomon receives God’s promises to David, those promises are fully realized only with the coming of Jesus Christ.

**blow the trumpet and say, “Long live King Solomon!”** A public celebration of Solomon’s new status as crown prince (cf. 1 Sam. 10:24; 2 Sam. 15:10; 16:16; 2 Kin. 9:13; 11:12), or perhaps David and Solomon have a co-regency for a short time.

Although made up of twelve tribes, the nation is composed of two major units, Israel in the north and Judah in the south. When David became king, he had to command assent from both Judah (2 Sam. 2:4) and Israel (2 Sam. 5:3). As heir to the Davidic dynasty, Solomon becomes king of both areas at once. This description may also highlight a long-standing division between the north and the south that later results in two separate monarchies at the death of Solomon.
See note on v. 8.

In ancient Israel both priests and prophets could officiate at the anointing of a king (1 Sam. 9:16; 16:12; 2 Kin. 9:1–3; 11:12).

**tent.** A reference to the tent David pitched (2 Sam. 6:17) to house the ark of the covenant (Ex. 37:1–9); not the same as the tabernacle of Moses (Ex. 35:4–29; 36:8–38; 1 Kin. 3:4; 1 Chr. 16:39; 21:29).
See note on v. 33.
David praises God (v. 48) because his prayer for succession has been granted (cf. Gen. 47:31).
The guests at Adonijah’s coronation festival are afraid because their attendance at the feast signifies that they are part of the rebellion.

These are projections resembling horns at the four corners on the top of the altar (Ex. 27:2; 29:12; Lev. 4:7; Ps. 118:27). The place of sacrifice is sacred, and Adonijah is seeking sanctuary there before God in the hope that he will not be killed (Ex. 21:12–14; 1 Kin. 2:28–34).

verse_quote: If he will show himself a worthy man.
note: Solomon spares Adonijah on condition that he conduct himself as a loyal citizen of Solomon’s kingdom.

David, like Jacob (Gen. 49), Moses (Deut. 31:1–8), Joshua (Josh. 23), and Samuel (1 Sam. 12) before him, gives a final speech before his death. These speeches mark the transition from one era to another and the transfer of authority.

verse_quote: the way of all the earth.
note:
A euphemism for death (Josh. 23:14).

**Be strong, and show yourself a man.** These instructions are suitable either before a warrior goes into battle or before a person undertakes a difficult task (Deut. 31:7, 23; Josh. 1:6, 7, 9, 18; 1 Sam. 4:9).

verse_quote: walking in his ways and keeping his statutes.
note: David admonishes Solomon to be faithful to God and so experience blessing (cf. Deut. 4:40; 6:2; 8:6, 11; 10:12–11:1).

verse_quote: If your sons pay close attention to their way.
note:
David’s instructions to Solomon echo God’s promises to David through the prophet Nathan in 2 Sam. 7:8–16 and reaffirmed in David’s prayer in 2 Sam. 7:18–29. Here David underscores the need for covenant faithfulness (cf. 8:25, 26; 9:4, 5).

**with all their heart and ... soul.** An allusion to Deut. 4:29 and 6:5. When Jesus is asked what is the greatest commandment, He likewise quotes from Deut. 6:5 (Matt. 22:35–40).

Joab is the most successful, but also the most unscrupulous, of David’s generals (1:7 note). David calls on Solomon to see to it that the crimes Joab has committed against his rivals Abner (2 Sam. 3:22–30) and Amasa (cf. 2 Sam. 20:4–10) do not go unpunished. The way Joab tricked Abner and Amasa and murdered them was unlawful (Deut. 19:1–13; 21:1–9). This may, in reality, be not mere vengeance on David’s part but a political move to protect Solomon from Joab, who is particularly dangerous, violent, and without scruples.
To enjoy a position of honor at the court and share in the bounty of the state (2 Sam. 9:7; 19:28; 2 Kin. 25:29; Neh. 5:17).
He cursed and stoned David, who was running from his son Absalom (2 Sam. 16:5–8). Shimei later begged for pardon, and David promised that Shimei would not die (2 Sam. 19:16–23).
Cursing a ruler violates God’s law (Ex. 22:28; cf. 1 Kin. 21:10).

One of David’s major accomplishments was to capture Jerusalem, which became the nation’s capital. The city afterward bore the name of David in his honor (2 Sam. 5:7). David’s city was located on a spur between the Central Valley and the Kidron Valley. Solomon later expanded the city to the north to include the Ophel and Mount Moriah, the site of the temple complex.
David ruled c. 1010–970 B.C.. During his last years he may have shared the throne with Solomon (1:38–40).

verse_quote: all Israel fully expected me to reign.
note:
This is wishful thinking on Adonijah’s part (1:7–10).

**it was his from the** LORD**.** Adonijah claims to recognize the sanctity of Solomon’s reign, but his request for Abishag suggests otherwise.

In the ancient Near East, a large court and family were a sign of royal status. Abishag remained a virgin while she stayed with David (1:1–4), so Adonijah would not be technically breaking the law by marrying her (Deut. 22:30). Nonetheless, should Adonijah prove successful in marrying Abishag from David’s harem, this might constitute a claim to the throne and an open affront to Solomon’s power (cf. 2 Sam. 3:6, 7; 12:7, 8; 16:20–24).

Bathsheba accedes to Adonijah’s request. It is unclear whether she has been taken in by Adonijah’s ruse or whether she is merely playing along, confident of what Solomon’s response will be. Adonijah’s caution suggests that he may not be looking to overthrow Solomon. By highlighting how Solomon breaks his word to his mother, the narrator implies that Solomon’s decision to execute Adonijah is an abuse of his royal power.
The “right” is a position of high honor (Ps. 110:1; Matt. 20:21).
Solomon likely considers Adonijah’s request to marry Abishag to be treasonous and an attempt to revive his conspiracy to take the throne.

See v. 12.

**a house, as he promised.** According to 1 Kin. 11:42 and 14:21, Solomon’s son Rehoboam was born about a year before Solomon comes to power (cf. 1 Chr. 22:9, 10).

Because Abiathar, as a holy priest, carried the ark (2 Sam. 15:24, 29) and shared David’s hardships (1 Sam. 22:20–23; 23:6–9; 30:7; 2 Sam. 17:15; 19:11), Solomon tempers the penalty he metes out to Abiathar, banishing him to Anathoth (his ancestral home). Anathoth was four miles (6 km) from Jerusalem.

The writer of Kings is fond of pointing out God’s fulfillment of earlier promises (8:20; 12:15; 15:29; 16:12). In this case, the prophecy of a man of God concerning the demise and removal of Eli’s descendants from priestly office (1 Sam. 2:30–36) is realized during the reign of Solomon.
Having heard of Adonijah’s execution and Abiathar’s banishment, Joab flees to “the tent of the LORD” (1:39 note), and grasps “the horns of the altar” (1:50 note) in the hope of escaping retribution.

Joab can find asylum at the altar only if he accidentally caused the death of another (Ex. 21:14). Instead, Joab’s role in Adonijah’s sedition gives Solomon the opportunity to honor one of his father’s last requests (vv. 5, 6; 1:7 note).
, **31** It seems likely that the narrator of Kings does not approve of Solomon’s command to kill Joab at the altar., 31

Despite their earlier loyalties to Saul and Absalom, Abner became commander of the army of Israel (2 Sam. 2:8, 9) and Amasa commander of the army of Judah (2 Sam. 19:13; 20:4–10). Joab killed them because he perceived them as threats to his control of the military.
Both Zadok and Abiathar played leading roles in Israel as priests appointed by David (2 Sam. 8:17 note). Zadok and his descendants now become the sole high priestly family in Israel (1 Sam. 2:35).

–**46** The execution of Shimei is the third death ordered by Solomon in this chapter. As with Adonijah and Joab, the narrator suggests that Solomon does not act wisely in having Shimei killed. Strictly speaking, Shimei does not disobey Solomon’s instruction in v. 37, for his journey to Gath does not take him across the Kidron Valley. In each case it can be argued that Solomon displays an inability to judge appropriately. Only after he receives wisdom from God does this change (3:16–28).
One of the five major Philistine cities (Josh. 13:3; 1 Sam. 21:10; 27:2).

The name of the pharaoh mentioned here is not known but could be one of the last monarchs of the Twenty-First Egyptian Dynasty. Though Egypt is not particularly powerful in Solomon’s day, this treaty marriage attests the international prominence of Israel during the period of the united monarchy.

When the Israelites entered the land of Canaan, they were supposed to destroy all the hilltop shrines of the Canaanites (Num. 33:52; Deut. 7:5; 12:3). Until the construction of the temple, Israel was allowed to worship at divinely sanctioned sites (Ex. 20:24; Judg. 6:24; 13:19; 1 Sam. 7:17; 9:12, 13). Solomon, however, continues the building of and worship at these sites even after the temple is built (11:7, 8), in disobedience to Deut. 12.
That is, the stipulations of the Mosaic covenant (2:3 note).

Chronicles says that the tabernacle of Moses and the ancient bronze altar were located at Gibeon (1 Chr. 21:29; 2 Chr. 1:2–6).

**burnt offerings.** Used for thanksgiving and atonement, the burnt offering was the most common type of offering. The animal was burned completely except for the hide, which was taken by the priest (Lev. 7:8).

This dream sets the stage for the first major period in Solomon’s tenure as king. For dreams as vehicles of revelation, see Gen. 26:24; 28:12; 31:11; 46:2; Num. 12:6; Judg. 7:13; Dan. 2:4; 7:1; Matt. 1:20; 2:12, 19, 22.
Solomon is young and inexperienced but is humble enough to admit it (cf. Jer. 1:6).

Since the exodus from Egypt, the Israelites have grown in population to the point that elements of the promises to Abraham (Gen. 12:2; 13:16; 22:17, 18) and Jacob (Gen. 32:12) are now being realized. This large population presents its leader with considerable challenges.
LORD**.** Solomon does not ask for the usual wishes of an oriental king: long life, wealth, or the death of his enemies (v. 11).
Solomon’s wisdom is incomparable in the history of Israel (4:29–34; 10:6–9).

verse_quote: if you will walk in my ways ... I will lengthen your days.
note: Unlike the other divine gifts, a long life is contingent upon Solomon’s continuing faithfulness to God—a condition he will fail to fulfill (11:1–13).
In gratitude to God, Solomon returns to Jerusalem, stands before the ark, the central symbol of God’s presence (Ex. 37:1–9), and offers burnt offerings (v. 4 note) and peace offerings (Lev. 3).
In the ancient Near East it was expected of a king that he would hear special cases and appeals (2 Sam. 14:4–21; 15:1–4). In this way the monarch was directly responsible to the people.
Prior to this, Solomon used the sword to avenge his and his father’s enemies. Now he uses it as a sign of his new character and wisdom.

verse_quote: give half to the one and half to the other.
note: A legal tradition in the ancient Near East stipulated that if a judge could not determine who owned a disputed piece of property, he should divide it evenly between the two contestants (cf. Ex. 21:35). Solomon’s application of this tradition in this case is brilliant.

verse_quote: they stood in awe of the king.
note: Solomon’s ruling demonstrates that God has indeed given him “wisdom ... to do justice” (cf. v. 12; Prov. 16:10).
Solomon, like David before him, rules over a united kingdom (1:35 note).

In Hebrew, the word “son” can mean “descendant” (Gen. 31:28, 43). In this case, Azariah is probably the son of Ahimaaz (1 Chr. 6:8, 9) and thus the grandson of Zadok the priest.

**the priest.** The use of the definite article indicates that Azariah is now the chief priest.

The two leading priests during the reign of David and the beginning of Solomon’s reign. Solomon deposes Abiathar for supporting Adonijah (1:7; 2:27), while Azariah succeeds Zadok as priest during the reign of Solomon (v. 2).

His identity is unclear. Possibilities include the prophet Nathan (2 Sam. 7:2–17; 12:1–15; 1 Kin. 1:11) and the son of David (2 Sam. 5:14).

**king’s friend.** That is, an advisor to the king (see 2 Sam. 15:37; 16:16).

This important post involves administering the palace and overseeing the king’s properties (1 Kin. 16:9; 18:3; 2 Kin. 18:18, 37; 19:2).

**Adoniram.** Also known as “Adoram,” he is in charge of forced labor during the reigns of David (2 Sam. 20:24), Solomon, and Rehoboam (12:18).

**forced labor.** This conscripted labor is performed primarily, but not exclusively, by captives of war from defeated nations (5:13–16; 9:15, 23; cf. Num. 31:25–47; Josh. 9:23).

The new administrative districts overseen by these governors are not exactly the same as the old Israelite tribal areas, possibly because the tribes vary greatly in population and land holdings, and Solomon desires a steady monthly income for his government. Each district is responsible to provide food for the royal court one month per year on an annual rotation.
This name has been discovered inscribed on a jar handle at khirbet Raddana from the twelfth century B.C..

For Sihon see Num. 32:33; Deut. 2:24–37. Subsequent to the Israelite capture of Sihon’s territory, the Israelites defeated King Og of Bashan and captured all his lands (east of the Sea of Chinneroth; see Num. 32:33; Deut. 3:1–11). Geber is therefore governor over a large district east of the Jordan.

verse_quote: as many as the sand by the sea.
note:
A fulfillment of the promises to the patriarchs (3:8 note; cf. Gen. 22:17; 32:12).

**ate ... drank ... happy.** Solomon’s economic policies produce prosperity for the nation.

Perhaps to be identified with Wadi el-Arish in northeastern Sinai. The borders of Solomon’s kingdom are in essence the borders promised to Abraham (Gen. 15:18; 17:8; Deut. 1:7; 11:24; Josh. 1:4). Hence, in the presentation of Kings, Solomon rules over an empire representing the long-awaited fulfillment of the patriarchal promises (cf. vv. 24, 25).
These are for Solomon’s court, palace, and extended family.

Tiphsah is located on the west bank of the Euphrates, and Gaza is located on the southeastern Mediterranean coast.

**peace on all sides.** David had to fight many wars to secure the kingdom, and Solomon enjoyed the result. Conditions of peace were a prerequisite for major building projects such as the temple and palace (2 Sam. 7:10, 11; 1 Kin. 5:3–5).

There are variations in the versions as to how many stalls for chariot horses Solomon had. If the “12,000 horsemen” means “12,000 horses” then each stall has three horses, the normal complement for a chariot being two primary horses and one reserve. According to 10:26, Solomon has 1,400 chariots. Solomon’s chariot force and bureaucracy require ample, regular provisions (vv. 27, 28).

That is, Mesopotamia to the northeast (Gen. 29:1) and Arabia to the east (Jer. 49:28; Ezek. 25:4, 10).

**Egypt.** Examples of wisdom literature from both Mesopotamia and Egypt have been discovered and translated.

Solomon is a lover and supporter of wisdom literature and is himself an accomplished author. In fact, the book of Proverbs opens with the words, “The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.”
Solomon takes a special interest in nature. By writing proverbs, Solomon gives order to social relations; by listing fauna and flora, he gives order to the elements of his kingdom.

Solomon acquires an international reputation for wisdom during his lifetime. The monarchs of various nations send emissaries to learn from Solomon’s erudition. The Ebla texts from 2350 B.C. mention learned men from many nations lecturing in Ebla, showing how early such travel was possible.

Tyre is a city on the Mediterranean coast, in modern-day Lebanon. Since Hiram ruled c. 980–947 B.C.., his reign overlaps both David’s and Solomon’s.

**Hiram always loved David.** Hiram supplied materials and workers when David built himself a palace (2 Sam. 5:11).

verse_quote: the warfare with which his enemies surrounded him.
note: Even though David wanted to build the temple himself, he spent much of his reign expanding and consolidating the kingdom (2 Sam. 7:10, 11). In a play on the Hebrew word for “house,” the prophet Nathan told David that God would build a “house,” or dynasty, for him, while David’s offspring would build a “house,” or temple, for God (2 Sam. 7:12–16). Through God’s grace, Solomon is implementing the promise made to his father David.
The rest that many of Israel’s leaders had hoped for (Ex. 33:14; Deut. 25:19; Josh. 1:13, 15; 2 Sam. 7:11) is now a reality.

LORD**.** In Semitic culture, a name is thought to reveal something of a person’s character and identity (Gen. 17:5; 32:28; Ex. 3:13, 14; 34:6, 7; Deut. 12:5). See 2 Sam. 7:13.

**Your son.** Solomon refers explicitly to God’s promise in 2 Sam. 7:12, 13.

These trees were famous in the ancient Near East and often used in building royal palaces and temples.

**no one ... who knows how.** The Israelites do not have the craftsmen and artisans needed to construct the temple by themselves.

**Sidonians.** Taken in a narrow sense, they are the residents of the port city of Sidon north of Tyre. Here the term probably refers to the inhabitants of Tyre, Gebal (Byblos), and Sidon, the people who are later called the “Phoenicians.”

verse_quote: Blessed be the LORD this day.
note: Even a foreign king acknowledges the accomplishments of Israel’s God manifested through King Solomon (cf. 10:6–9).
In exchange for Hiram’s help, Solomon is expected to supply food for Hiram’s court (v. 11) and wages for his workers (v. 6).
Solomon’s administrative and political talents are again associated with God’s gift of wisdom. (cf. Deut. 1:15; Is. 11:2–4).

verse_quote: drafted forced labor out of all Israel.
note: Solomon presses some of his own people into service as forced laborers on his building projects. This policy is deeply resented and contributes in no small way to the division of the kingdom after Solomon’s death (9:22; 12:4, 16 and notes).
See note on 4:6.

A likely reference to the ashlar masonry used in royal Israelite architecture of the period of the united monarchy. The use of such building materials and methods is an indicator of material prosperity.
In this era, Gebal (or Byblos) is known internationally for its trade in papyrus, the ancient form of paper made from pressed and dried cuttings of papyrus reed.

The author’s chronology reflects how momentous the construction of the temple is for Israel’s life under God. The building of the temple under Solomon is the culmination of a long series of events that began with the deliverance out of Egypt.

**fourth year of Solomon’s reign.** Approximately 966 B.C., placing the exodus in the year 1446 B.C.. Some scholars date the exodus in the thirteenth century B.C.. They understand four hundred eighty years in one of two ways. Some take it as a figurative number representing twelve generations of forty years each. Others, on the basis of ancient Near Eastern custom, argue that the figure is the total of a sequence of periods, some of them overlapping.

LORD**.** There are a number of similarities between the tabernacle and the temple, although the temple is twice the size of the tabernacle (Ex. 26:15–30; 36:20–34). Both are divided into three main sections: a vestibule, a sanctuary (the Holy Place), and an inner sanctuary (the Most Holy Place). This three-part structure is common in other ancient Near Eastern temples. Israel’s sanctuary differs radically from a pagan sanctuary because it has no idols or standing stones. At its center is the ark of the covenant containing the Ten Commandments, the moral will of God that orders Israel’s life (Deut. 10:4, 5; 1 Kin. 8:6–9).
Wide on the inner side of the wall, these windows gradually slope to form a slit on the outer wall.
These rooms surround the Most Holy Place and the Holy Place but not the vestibule. They are used for storage.
The total height of the three stories of side rooms is not as high as the main temple itself.
That is, of the side rooms (see text note).

verse_quote: if you will walk in my statutes.
note: With special reference to the building of the temple, God reminds Solomon that the promises to David require covenant fidelity on Solomon’s part (2:3, 4 and notes).

The existence of the temple does not guarantee the presence of God with Israel. Loyalty to the Torah born of Israel’s trust only in the Lord is the main issue in the people’s relationship with God (cf. 2:3 note; 9:6–9).

verse_quote: an inner sanctuary, as the Most Holy Place.
note: The Most Holy Place, a perfect cube about thirty feet (9 m) on a side (v. 20), is the most sacred area of the temple. It contains the ark of the covenant (v. 19) and the cherubim. Only the high priest is allowed to enter this room and then only on one day a year, the Day of Atonement (Heb. _Yom Kippur;_ Lev. 16; 23:26–32; Num. 29:7–11). The tabernacle has a Most Holy Place (Ex. 26:33; cf. Heb. 9:12).

verse_quote: the ark of the covenant of the
note: LORD**.** The central symbol of the Israelite’s communion with God, the ark contains the two tablets of the covenant (Ex. 25:21; Deut. 9:9).
The temple is beautiful and costly. In its glory and beauty, this earthly temple resembles God’s heavenly temple (8:36, 39; Heb. 9:11, 23, 24).

verse_quote: altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary.
note: Probably an incense altar (7:48; cf. Ex. 30:1, 6; 37:25–28; Heb. 9:4).

Winged creatures with human faces (cf. Gen. 3:24; Ezek. 41:18, 19), the two cherubim stand as guardians on either side of the ark (8:6, 7; 2 Chr. 3:10–13). The tips of their unfolded wings reached ten cubits high, or half the height of the Most Holy Place itself (v. 16). In the ancient Near East, kings were sometimes depicted as sitting upon a throne supported by cherubim. The cherubim in the temple may represent God’s symbolic enthronement in the Most Holy Place. God is present with His people and associates Himself in a special way with this place of worship (1 Sam. 4:4; 6:2; 1 Kin. 8:10–13; 2 Kin. 19:15; Ps. 80:1; 99:1).

An image reminiscent of the garden of Eden in Gen. 2. Though our first ancestors were expelled from Paradise because of their rebellion against God (Gen. 3:24), and we share their expulsion, communion with God is still possible through His grace.

Part of the exterior courtyard surrounding the temple, where the great altar and the molten sea are situated (cf. 7:23–26). Access to this area nearest the temple itself seems to be restricted to the priests (2 Chr. 4:9).

**three courses.** Each layer of stone is separated by a layer of cedar beams (cf. Ezra 6:4). Similar constructions have been unearthed at Megiddo.

It takes Solomon seven years to build the temple, whereas it takes him thirteen years to build his palace (7:1). That it takes Solomon longer to build his own palace suggests a concern for his glory that rivals his concern for the glory of the Lord.

verse_quote: the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
note:
Probably so named because of the extensive use of Lebanon cedar inside. This complex includes an armory (10:16, 17) and is probably located immediately south of the temple.

**length ... a hundred cubits and its breadth fifty ... and its height thirty.** Although the same height as the temple, Solomon’s palace is considerably longer and more than twice as wide (6:2).
Half the length of the palace and about two-thirds of the width (7:2), this colonnade is probably an impressive entrance hall.
The place where Solomon formally carries out his duties as administrator of God’s holy kingdom (3:16 note).

This part of the account is not placed chronologically; Solomon actually begins making arrangements for equipping the temple before to its actual completion (2 Chr. 2:7, 13, 14).

**7:13 Hiram.** He should not be confused with Hiram the king of Tyre with whom Solomon has ratified a treaty for the supply of materials and craftsmen (5:1–12). This Hiram is of mixed lineage: his father is a native of Tyre, but his mother is an Israelite.

verse_quote: full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze.
note: This resembles the description of Bezalel, who oversaw the construction of the tabernacle (Ex. 31:2, 3; 35:30, 31).

One pillar is on each side of the temple’s entrance (v. 21). They are called Jachin and Boaz. It is unclear whether they are freestanding or whether they support a roof that may also cover the porch of the temple.
It was common in the ancient Near East to lavish capitals with ornate decoration.

A huge circular basin holding up to eight thousand gallons (30,283 L) of water (2 Chr. 4:5 note). According to Chronicles, the priests use the sea for cleansing (2 Chr. 4:6). Its symbolic significance is disputed. Some scholars highlight the positive attributes of water as life-giving, while others argue that the bronze sea commemorates God’s power over the forces of chaos, typified by the sea (cf. Rev. 21:1).

The sea rests on four triads of oxen pointed in the four cardinal directions. In the ancient Near East, oxen symbolized physical and reproductive potency. Their arrangement is indicative of God’s universal lordship.
These portable and highly decorated wagons hold water basins (v. 38). The priests use the water to wash sections of animals that have been slaughtered for burnt offerings (Lev. 1:9, 13; 2 Chr. 4:6).
Priests use the shovels to remove ashes from the altar and the bowls for rituals involving blood or water (Ex. 27:3; Jer. 52:18).
This center of metallurgy is located east of the Jordan, north of the Wadi Jabbok (Gen. 33:17; Josh. 13:27; Judg. 8:4, 5). Zarethan is nearby.

The same altar described in 6:22. The bread of the Presence or holy bread (1 Sam. 21:4, 6) arranged on the golden table is understood as an offering before God (Ex. 25:23–30; Lev. 24:5–9; Num. 4:7; 2 Chr. 13:11; Matt. 12:4).
There are ten lampstands in the temple as compared to only one in the tabernacle (Ex. 25:31–40; 26:35).

During his reign, David accumulated booty from military campaigns and received tribute from a variety of states (2 Sam. 8:9–12; 1 Chr. 18:7–11; 2 Chr. 5:1).

**treasuries of the house of the** LORD**.** Depositories for the government’s wealth, sometimes used as tribute by the kings to ward off foreign invaders (15:18; 2 Kin. 12:18; 18:13–16). The treasure is also the object of raids by opposing kings (14:25, 26; 2 Kin. 14:13, 14).

Senior leaders who are in charge of local government and justice throughout OT history (Ex. 18:13–26; Num. 11:16–30; Judg. 21:16–24; 1 Sam. 8:1–9).

**the city of David, which is Zion.** This oldest section of Jerusalem is south of the temple. David earlier brought the ark from the house of Obed-edom in Baale-judah to Zion (2 Sam. 6:1–19).

Solomon apparently waits eleven months to dedicate the temple (6:38) so that the ceremony can be part of the Feast of Booths in the New Year, which is commemorated during the seventh month (Lev. 23:34; Deut. 16:13–15).
The tabernacle along with all its furnishings is brought, presumably from Gibeon (3:4 note), by the priests and the Levites.

verse_quote: underneath the wings of the cherubim.
note: See note on 6:23.
Statements to this effect (9:13, 21; 10:12; 12:19) are written from the perspective of a writer who lived before the destruction of the temple (586 B.C.). See Introduction: Author.

The copy of the Ten Commandments (cf. v. 21; Ex. 34:1; Deut. 9:11).

**Horeb.** The name of the region within which Mount Sinai stands.

verse_quote: a cloud filled the house of the
note: LORD**.** After the exodus from Egypt, God led His people through the wilderness with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night (Ex. 13:21; 40:36–38). At Mount Sinai, God revealed Himself in a cloud (Ex. 19:9; 24:15–18). When the tabernacle was constructed, God covered it with the cloud and filled it with His glory (Ex. 40:34, 35; cf. Lev. 16:2). Now He shows His approval of the newly constructed sanctuary by appearing in this cloud theophany.
No one can see God and live, but God can reveal Himself and manifest His love toward His people in indirect ways (v. 10 note). Cf. the thick darkness in Ex. 20:21; Deut. 4:11; and 5:22.

verse_quote: a place for you to dwell in forever.
note: The temple, as a divinely sanctioned place for prayer and sacrifice, is the place of God’s presence among His people (Pss. 76:2; 132:13, 14; Is. 8:18; Amos 1:2).
This gesture signifies prayer (Ex. 9:29; Is. 1:15; 1 Tim. 2:8).

verse_quote: there is no God like you.
note: The incomparability of God is a prominent theme throughout the Scriptures (Ex. 15:11; Deut. 4:39; Ps. 86:8; Mark 12:29–32; Eph. 4:6; Rev. 19:6). God’s fidelity is not temporary (3:6; 8:16; Deut. 7:9, 12; Ps. 52:8; Heb. 13:8), nor is His power limited to a specific country (vv. 41–43; Jon. 1:9).

verse_quote: if only your sons pay close attention.
note: Solomon repeats the condition that his dynasty will continue to rule Israel only if David’s descendants remain faithful to God (2:3, 4; 6:11–13; 9:4–9; 11:11–13).
God promised that He would be present in a special way in the Jerusalem temple, and Solomon implores God to hear the prayers that are directed toward the temple (Dan. 6:10; 9:17; Jon. 2:4).

In certain trials the suspect might be required to take an oath of innocence at the sanctuary to corroborate his defense (Ex. 22:7–12; Num. 5:11–31). Solomon prays that God, through His involvement in the suspects’ lives, will condemn the guilty and declare the innocent not guilty (v. 32).

verse_quote: because they have sinned against you.
note: Not a defeat by an enemy’s god, but a defeat of Israel by God Himself due to Israel’s infidelity (Deut. 28:25; Josh. 7; 2 Chr. 36:15–19; Lam. 2:1–8).

verse_quote: bring them again to the land.
note: During Solomon’s time, it is not unusual for the army and people defeated in war to be deported to another land. Solomon asks God to be merciful and restore those who ask His forgiveness.
Just as God directs the fate of His people in war, so also God controls the world of nature. Drought is a curse of the covenant (17:1; cf. Deut. 11:16, 17; 28:22–24; Amos 4:7, 8).
Solomon lists a wide variety of afflictions: famine, pestilence, locusts, war, and sickness, all mentioned in Deut. 28.

verse_quote: render to each ... according to all his ways.
note: Solomon prays that God would use His infinite knowledge to establish justice among His people.

verse_quote: that all the peoples of the earth may know your name.
note: Solomon prays that one day all peoples would commit their lives to God, just as Israel does (cf. Is. 56:6–8; Zech. 8:23; Matt. 28:19).

verse_quote: If your people go out to battle.
note: Solomon is referring to military endeavors taken at divine behest (20:13–30; cf. Lev. 26:7; Deut. 20; 21:10; 1 Sam. 23:2, 4; 2 Sam. 5:19, 24).

verse_quote: no one who does not sin.
note:
See theological note “Human Depravity” on p. 889.

**they are carried away captive.** Exile from the land is one of the most severe curses in the Sinaitic covenant (v. 33 note; Lev. 26:33–45; Deut. 28:64–68; 30:1–5). Exile is also a curse in a number of ancient Near Eastern treaties.

Being outside the land of Israel does not mean that God’s promises are no longer operative (Neh. 1:11). Solomon beseeches God to cause the exiles’ captors to show mercy toward their captives (Ps. 106:46).

Since God specifically chose Israel and liberated that nation from Egypt to become His special inheritance (Ex. 19:3–6; Deut. 4:20; 9:26), Solomon prays that God will not forget this history of redemption when Israel is in exile.

verse_quote: the LORD who has given rest to his people.
note: After considerable upheaval in the period of wilderness wandering and conquest, Israel has experienced the fulfillment of what God had promised through His servant Moses (5:4 note; Ex. 33:14; Deut. 12:10). In the NT, where we see the Lord’s fulfillment of his promises all the more, Christians are exhorted to make every effort to enter God’s rest (Heb. 4:11; cf. Rev. 14:13).
The other gods that people worship are fabricated; the only real God is the God of Israel (cf. Deut. 4:35).

Over the course of fourteen days of dedicatory festivities, Solomon and the multitude of people present in Jerusalem offer a multitude of sacrifices, far more than at the comparatively modest dedication of the second temple (Ezra 6:16–18).

For burnt offerings, see note on 3:4. Grain offerings often accompanied animal sacrifices (Lev. 2; 7:11–14; 8:26–28; 9:4; 14:20; Num. 15:1–10) and are indications of the worshiper’s gratitude and praise. For peace offerings, see Lev. 3.

**the bronze altar.** This altar on which sacrifices are burned is located in front of the temple (vv. 22, 54) and is different from the incense altar inside the temple (6:22 note).

A city in central Syria located on the Orontes River approximately fifteen miles (24 km) directly east of Byblos.

**Brook of Egypt.** See 4:21.

verse_quote: all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.
note: God has graciously fulfilled His commitment to David that one of his offspring would build the temple he wanted to build (2 Sam. 7:1–16). God also gives Israel a central sanctuary (Deut. 12) and rest from their enemies (1 Kin. 5:4).
The first appearance of God to Solomon was at Gibeon, where the Lord asked the king what He could give to him (3:5).
God has made the temple holy by being present in a special way (8:10–13, 29).

The attention shifts to the conduct of Solomon and future kings. As stated previously (2:3, 4 and notes; 8:25), the future dominion of David’s descendants over Israel is contingent on their fidelity to the Torah.

The presence of the temple is not an unchangeable guarantee against the consequences of prolonged covenant infidelity (6:13 note). The covenant curses will come into effect if the king and people are unfaithful (Deut. 28:37; Jer. 19:8). Disobedience and apostasy will result in exile from the land of promise.
Other peoples will understand the cause of the unusual spectacle of God destroying His own temple and exiling His people (Deut. 29:24–28).

This section highlights Solomon’s glory by summarizing his building projects (9:10–28), his fame (10:1–13), and his great riches (10:14–29).

**9:10 At the end of twenty years.** Given the earlier chronological notices (6:1, 37, 38; 7:1), this occurs c. 946 B.C..

verse_quote: Solomon gave to Hiram twenty cities.
note: Although Solomon and Hiram made an earlier agreement (5:1–12), it appears that Solomon is now in financial difficulty. In exchange for Hiram sending Solomon 120 talents (four-and-a-half tons) of gold (v. 14), Solomon grants Hiram twenty cities in Galilee (cf. 2 Chr. 8:2 and note).

This name perhaps reflects a Hebrew construction that means “as not” or “as good as nothing.” Another possibility is that it stems from a Hebrew verb that means “to fetter” (cf. Ps. 149:8), and thus Hiram believes that he has been shackled with towns of dubious worth.

At first glance, this seems like a huge amount of gold. Nevertheless, the gold Solomon receives from Hiram is not as much as the 150 talents of gold Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria later claims to receive from Tyre c. 730 B.C.. Solomon’s accumulation of gold is emphasized throughout his reign (9:28; 10:22).

As the city of Jerusalem expanded northward along the Ophel ridge, it was necessary to build supporting earthworks for the city’s fortifications. The Millo (lit. “filling”) was apparently such a restraining structure constructed east of the palace to fill in a depression along the top of the ridge (v. 24; 11:27; cf. 2 Sam. 5:9; 2 Kin. 12:20; 2 Chr. 32:5). Archaeologists have uncovered a stepped-stone structure on the Ophel ridge that perhaps served as the Millo.

**Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer.** These towns are strategically located along major trade routes. Hazor is ten miles (16 km) north of the Sea of Chinneroth (Galilee); Megiddo is at the opening onto the Jezreel Valley of a strategic pass through the Carmel ridge. Gezer is twenty miles (32 km) west of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavation has revealed identical Solomonic gates and outer-wall systems at each of these sites. By fortifying these three sites, Solomon has consolidated his control of trade and commerce.

verse_quote: Pharaoh ... had gone up and captured Gezer.
note: Gezer remained in Canaanite hands, despite the Israelite conquest (Josh. 16:10; Judg. 1:29). The pharaoh captured Gezer, perhaps from the Philistines. Since Egypt and Israel have a treaty (3:1), it is in the interest of both countries not to have Gezer in hostile hands.
Eleven miles (18 km) northwest of Jerusalem (cf. Josh. 16:3) at the foot of a strategic pass controlling access to the Judean highlands.

Eight miles (13 km) northeast of Ashdod, near the Mediterranean coast (cf. Josh. 19:44).

**Tamar.** Sixteen miles (26 km) southwest of the Dead Sea (Judg. 1:16). Tamar means “palm” (Ezek. 47:19; 48:28).

**in the wilderness, in the land of Judah.** Excavators have discovered a series of fortresses in the northern Negev built during the reign of Solomon to serve, in particular, against an invasion from Egypt.

verse_quote: the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
note: When Israel entered the land of Canaan, they were to destroy completely the nations living there (Deut. 7:1, 2; 20:17; Josh. 3:10; 9:1). The Israelites did not do this in any systematic fashion (Josh. 16:10; Judg. 1, 2; 3:5), and Solomon’s policy is to conscript the descendants of these peoples permanently (v. 21).
Solomon conscripts permanently foreign peoples living in the land, but the Israelite workers he conscripts serve for fixed periods of time (5:13 note; 12:4 note).

So as not to be dependent on the merchant navies and ports of other nations, Solomon builds ships at Ezion-geber, his own port. This is a new venture for Israel, and Solomon enlists the help of his ally Hiram of Tyre, who supplies sailors to accompany Solomon’s own (v. 27).

**Red Sea.** Here, the Gulf of Aqaba (Jer. 49:20, 21).
The location of Ophir is disputed (Job 28:16; Ps. 45:9; Is. 13:12). Suggestions include western Arabia, the Horn of Africa, and India.

Two main suggestions for this location are southwest Arabia (modern Yemen) and northern Arabia, the land of the Sabeans (Job 1:15; 6:19; Ps. 72:10).

**concerning the name of the** LORD**.** The queen of Sheba comes to Jerusalem not simply because of Solomon’s fame but because she recognizes the relationship between Solomon’s fame and the Lord.

**hard questions.** Wishing to discover whether Solomon’s reputation is deserved, the queen of Sheba tests him with hard questions (cf. Judg. 14:12).

See notes on 2:7 and 4:22.

**his cupbearers.** The cupbearer was an important post in ancient Near Eastern governments (Gen. 40; 41:9; Neh. 1:11).

verse_quote: Blessed be the LORD your God.
note: The queen of Sheba specifically mentions the personal name of the God of Israel in her statement to Solomon (vv. 6–9). Jesus cites the queen of Sheba in His indictment against the people of His own day (Matt. 12:42; Luke 11:31).

In addition to helping build Solomon’s fleet, Hiram of Tyre uses some of his own ships to transport goods for Solomon (9:26–28; 10:22).

**almug wood.** Suggestions about the nature of this wood include red sandalwood and juniper. It was apparently quite valuable and rare.

verse_quote: lyres and harps for the singers.
note: Israelite royalty probably sponsored musicians to compose appropriate hymns and psalms for worship.
They exchange gifts (v. 10).

verse_quote: came to Solomon in one year.
note: Annual, steady tribute is necessary to support all of Solomon’s major projects and outlays.

Solomon controls a large territory on the trade routes north to Mesopotamia and south to Egypt. Tariffs on the goods transported through Israel are substantial.

**governors of the land.** See 4:7–19.

These extremely heavy and valuable shields are made chiefly for ceremonial and aesthetic reasons. The use of such shields as a visible sign of a king’s wealth and status is not unique to Solomon. After a campaign dated c. 714 B.C., King Sargon II claimed to have taken “six shields of gold” from a temple., 17

Solomon uses the great influx of tribute to support an extravagant lifestyle (vv. 18–21, 23–25). His throne is probably made of wood inlaid with ivory and gold. Ivory carvings plated with gold have been found in the Assyrian royal palaces at Nimrud. Solomon’s desire for the finest in furnishings and buildings burdens his subjects (12:4).

Beautiful golden vessels from ancient times have been found in Egypt (thirteenth century B.C.), Ugarit (on the Mediterranean coast in modern Syria, thirteenth century B.C..), and Persia (sixth to fourth centuries B.C..).

These so-called ships of Tarshish are built to make long ocean voyages.

**Tarshish.** Perhaps to be identified with Tartessos, located in modern-day Spain on the very western end of the Mediterranean Sea (Jon. 1:3).

**with the fleet of Hiram.** See note on 9:26.
The “law of the king” in Deut. 17:16 forbids the monarch to accumulate great numbers of chariots and horses from Egypt.
It is possible that Solomon finances the buildup of his military forces by his trading in the famous Cilician horses and the superior chariots of Egypt (v. 29).

Not only does Solomon amass chariots and horses; he also initiates substantial trade in these commodities through “the king’s traders” (v. 28). In doing this, Solomon is exploiting Israel’s strategic geographic location.

**the kings of the Hittites.** The Hittites live in Anatolia (Asia Minor). During Solomon’s reign they are no longer the unified empire they were between 1375 and 1240 B.C. In Solomon’s day, they are ruled by a number of minor kings, each with his own domain.

Whereas in the first part of his reign, “Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father” (3:3), he later “loved many foreign women.” Diplomatic marriages between the dynasties of various kingdoms were common in the ancient Near East as a means of ratifying treaties, but Deut. 17:17 forbids the multiplication of royal wives in Israel. Moreover, there are prohibitions against marrying foreign wives in Canaan (Ex. 34:16; Deut. 7:1–4; Josh. 23:12, 13).
Alludes to the warning of Deut. 7:4.

verse_quote: as was the heart of David his father.
note: David is consistently presented as a model king (3:14; 9:4; 14:8; 15:3; 2 Kin. 8:19; 22:2). He was not without sin (2 Sam. 11; 12; 24:1–15; 1 Kin. 15:5), but when he sinned, his repentance was exemplary (2 Sam. 12:16, 17; 24:10–17). David’s devotion to God was unparalleled.

The Phoenician goddess of love and fertility, called Astarte by the Greeks (cf. Judg. 2:13; 2 Kin. 23:13).

**Milcom.** Or Molech. He was the national god of the Ammonites and was associated with child sacrifice (Lev. 18:21).

Solomon’s many sins violate fundamental principles of Israelite religion: multiplying wives (v. 1 note), worshiping other gods (Ex. 20:3, 5), and building sanctuaries for foreign deities (vv. 7, 8; cf. Ex. 20:4). Throughout 1 and 2 Kings, monarchs are judged by whether they do what is right or what is evil in the eyes of the Lord (e.g., 1 Kin. 15:11, 26, 34).
The national god of the Moabites (2 Kin. 3:26, 27).
See vv. 29–39.

verse_quote: I will not do it in your days.
note: God’s great love for David causes Him to temper His judgment on Solomon in two respects: first, God postpones the division until the reign of Solomon’s son; second, God does not remove the entire kingdom from the Davidic dynasty (v. 13).

This probably refers to Judah (12:20; 2 Kin. 17:18). If Judah is already assumed and therefore not mentioned, another tribe is meant, such as Benjamin (12:21) or Simeon, which was allocated territory within the region settled by Judah (Josh. 19:1).

**for the sake of Jerusalem.** Jerusalem is God’s chosen city, the site of Israel’s central sanctuary anticipated in Deut. 12 and constructed by Solomon. Jerusalem is a central symbol of God’s love for His people and the communion between God and His people throughout the Bible (Pss. 68:29; 122:2–6; 135:21; 137:5–7; Is. 62:1; Dan. 9:25; Rev. 3:12; 21:2, 10).
See 2 Sam. 8:14. An earlier victory by Joab is reversed, as Hadad returns from exile in Egypt and successfully rebels against Solomon (v. 25).

The Midianites live east of Moab and Edom.

**Paran.** This area is in the Sinai peninsula southeast of Kadesh.

**gave him a house.** Taking notice of the emerging power of David’s dynasty, Pharaoh has sheltered David’s foes in the hope that one day they will curtail Israel’s power (v. 21). Ancient treaties forbade providing asylum to political rebels.
Following David’s death, Hadad wanted to return to his own land, despite the pharaoh’s objections, probably because he wanted to liberate it from Israelite domination (v. 25).

Formerly Solomon could boast that in his reign there was “neither adversary nor misfortune” (5:4), but now God has afflicted him with a succession of enemies.

**Hadadezer king of Zobah.** On David’s conquest of Hadadezer and Syria, see 2 Sam. 8:3–6; 10:15–19.
From his base in Damascus, Rezon persistently causes trouble for Solomon.

Jeroboam rebels against Solomon and escapes to Egypt until Solomon’s death.

**11:26 Jeroboam the son of Nebat ... against the king.** Whereas Hadad and Rezon are external enemies raised up by God, Jeroboam, an Ephraimite, is an internal foe.

**Zeredah.** Twenty-one miles (34 km) east of Joppa in the territory of Ephraim.
See note on 9:15.

verse_quote: over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.
note: Jeroboam is in charge of the laborers Solomon drafted from the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (5:13–16) and is well aware of the resentment these tribes feel toward Solomon (12:4).
Shiloh is in Ephraim, about twelve miles (19 km) east of Zeredah.

Ahijah performs a symbolic action, that is, he acts out a parable. Such colorful actions dramatize the reality of the spoken word and God’s intervention in history (22:11; cf. Is. 20; Jer. 13:1–11). In this case, the torn pieces of Ahijah’s robe illustrate the impending division of the kingdom.

On behalf of the Lord, Ahijah summons Jeroboam to take ten of the twelve pieces, symbolizing the ten northern tribes over which Jeroboam will shortly become king. As with the earlier rebellions of Hadad and Rezon, Jeroboam’s insurrection is a divine judgment against Solomon.
See note on v. 13.
See note on v. 12.
That is, from Solomon’s successor, Rehoboam (12:1–24).

verse_quote: that David my servant may always have a lamp.
note: The metaphor of a lamp signifies the permanence of the Davidic dynasty in the city of Jerusalem (15:4; cf. 2 Sam. 21:17; 2 Kin. 8:19; 2 Chr. 21:7; Ps. 132:17). God’s commitment to David will have a profound effect on the future survival of the Davidic dynasty (2 Sam. 7:8–16).

verse_quote: over all that your soul desires.
note:
A similar promise is given to David (2 Sam. 3:21).

**king over Israel.** That is, over the ten northern tribes. During the period of the divided kingdom, the term “Israel” most often designates these ten tribes. “Judah” denotes the domain still ruled by David’s descendants.

verse_quote: listen to all that I command you.
note:
Jeroboam will be subject to the same covenantal stipulations that were operative for Saul, David, and Solomon (2:3, 4 and notes).

**I will be with you.** An assurance of God’s presence and sustenance (Deut. 31:8; Judg. 2:18; 6:12, 16; 1 Sam. 3:19; 2 Sam. 5:10; 7:9). Ahijah hopes that Jeroboam will be more loyal to the covenant than Solomon was.

This phrase looks forward to a restoration of Davidic power. Such a restoration is later attempted by Josiah of Judah, but he is unable to complete it (2 Kin. 22; 23). The prophets also look for a renewal of Davidic rule (Jer. 30:9; Ezek. 34:23; 37:15–28; Hos. 3:5; Amos 9:11). These hopes are fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Messiah (Matt. 1:1; Mark 1:1).

Shishak, or Shoshenk I, was the first king over the Twenty-Second Dynasty and ruled 945–924 B.C. (14:25, 26). For many years before his rule, Egypt had been weak. But under his direction Egypt began to increase in power. Later Shishak attacked the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, recording the invasion on the walls of the temple at Karnak.

verse_quote: the Book of the Acts of Solomon.
note: One of the sources (no longer in existence) used by the writer of 1 and 2 Kings. Other official sources are mentioned in 14:19, 29.
Approximately 970–930 B.C..
See 2:10. This is idiomatic for burial. Common burials in ancient Israel were familial and generational.

King Rehoboam’s refusal to listen to the people’s request to lighten their burdens sparks secession by the northern tribes. From this point on, the northern kingdom is usually referred to as Israel and the southern kingdom as Judah.

**12:1 Shechem.** This major Israelite center associated with the renewal of the covenant with the Lord (Josh. 24:1–33) is in northern Ephraim, thirty miles (48 km) north of Jerusalem. The city is located on the central ridge road or “spin” that in ancient times went from Shechem in the north to Hebron in the south. The route was a commonly used thoroughfare from the time of the patriarchs (Gen. 35:27).

**to make him king.** Rehoboam travels to Shechem to be made king by acclamation (see 1 Sam. 11:15 and the covenant the northern tribes made with David in 2 Sam. 5:1–3). As it turns out, the northern tribes do not accept Rehoboam.

verse_quote: as soon as Jeroboam ... heard of it.
note: That is, about the death of Solomon (11:43) and the subsequent attempt of Rehoboam to become king over all Israel.

verse_quote: Your father made our yoke heavy.
note: The expression “yoke” is characteristically used for the oppression of the Israelites by foreign rulers (Lev. 26:13; Deut. 28:48; Is. 9:4; 10:27; 14:25; Jer. 27:8, 11; Ezek. 34:27). Its use here is an indictment of Solomon for imposing harsh labor on his own people (5:13; 9:22; 11:28 and notes).
These older and experienced advisors are well acquainted with the traditions of Israel and understand how the monarchy affects the lives of ordinary Israelites.

verse_quote: If you will be a servant.
note: Though entrusted with power, the Israelite king is to establish justice and so serve both God and His people (Deut. 17:14–20; Ps. 72).
These young advisors, like Rehoboam himself, have grown up in the royal court. Apparently they think that Rehoboam’s privileges are inalienable, like those of an oriental monarch.

verse_quote: My little finger is thicker than my father’s thighs.
note: An arrogant and unwise boast about how much more oppressive Rehoboam’s yoke will be than his father’s (v. 11).
By making reference to this deadly arachnid, Rehoboam is telling the people that he will increase their oppression.
LORD**.** God’s agency is no excuse for Rehoboam’s foolishness. Rather, God is using Rehoboam’s misguided actions as an instrument for fulfilling Ahijah’s prophecy (11:31–39).

verse_quote: Look now to your own house, David.
note: “David” refers to the dynasty of David. The northern tribes secede from Judah and from the authority of David’s descendants. For an identical taunt against David himself, see 2 Sam. 20:1.
That is, members of the northern tribes who have settled in the south.

Rehoboam unwisely sends out the chief of forced labor to quell the uprising (4:6; 5:14, where the name is given as Adoniram), and to reimpose oppressive conditions.

**all Israel.** Representatives of the northern tribes (12:1).
See note on 8:8.
Jeroboam does not seem to play an active role in the assembly at Shechem. Once he is made king, however, he takes charge over Israelite affairs (vv. 25–33).
This common expression designates a prophet (1 Sam. 2:27; 1 Kin. 13:1; 2 Kin. 4:7).
Probably a reference to members of the northern tribes who have settled in Judah (v. 17) and sojourners living in that tribal area.

verse_quote: return to his home, for this thing is from me.
note: The prophet Shemaiah reaffirms what the prophet Ahijah earlier declared (11:29–39): the division of the kingdom conforms to the will of God. The existence of two realms is ordained by God, and each now has the opportunity to prove its loyalty to His covenant.

In an effort to retain the people’s loyalty, Jeroboam makes golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and institutes an alternative (and forbidden) system of worship for Israel.

note: This is the form of assurance given before battles when the Lord is about to fight on Israel’s side (Josh. 6:2, 16; 8:1, 18; Judg. 7:2; 18:10; 2 Chr. 13:16; 16:8). God defends the cause of His people against oppressors and enemies (Ex. 15:1–21; Judg. 5; Hab. 3:3–19; Rev. 18).
The thirty-two kings are overconfident and callous about their responsibilities.

verse_quote: Their gods are gods of the hills.
note:
Both Samaria and Jerusalem are located in the central hill country. In the polytheistic conceptions of the time, each god has specific zones of influence and strengths.

**fight against them in the plain.** It is understood that wars are fought not only by armies but also by their gods, and the Syrians want to fight in the plains where they think Yahweh will be outside His sphere of influence and hence in a weak position.
The kings have been getting drunk (vv. 12, 16), and it is wise to replace them with fighting men.
About four miles (6 km) east of the Sea of Chinneroth (Galilee).

verse_quote: the kings of ... Israel are merciful.
note:
Certain powers in the Near East, such as Assyria, were brutal toward the vanquished.

**sackcloth ... ropes.** The Syrians are dramatizing their humility and submission to the Israelites.

Earlier, Ahab addressed Ben-hadad as a superior (vv. 4, 9); now the tables have turned.

**He is my brother.** Ahab’s surprising response depicts Ben-hadad as an equal in a treaty relationship (9:13), a concession Ben-hadad’s men are quick to exploit (v. 33).

International trade can bring substantial income (10:23–29), and the guarantee of a market in another country affords a distinct economic advantage for the merchants of Israel.

**these terms.** The two kings formalize their negotiations by ratifying a covenant or treaty.
This designation does not mean physical children but members of a prophetic guild or association. Elijah and Elisha are probably leaders of such groups (2 Kin. 2:3, 15; 4:1, 38; 6:1; 9:1).

verse_quote: Because you have not obeyed the ...
note:
LORD**.** This highly unusual incident needs to be understood in the context of the previous story in which Ahab did not obey the dictates of holy war. Aware of Ahab’s treaty with Ben-hadad II, the prophet is dramatizing the consequences of refusing to heed the word of God.

**a lion shall strike you.** The old prophet from Bethel earlier uttered a similar decree of judgment against the man of God from Judah (13:20–25).
Ahab shows no mercy and so passes judgment on himself (v. 42; cf. 2 Sam. 12:1–15a, where Nathan says that David has passed judgment on himself).

verse_quote: whom I had devoted to destruction.
note:
See Lev. 27:28; Josh. 6:17; 7:1, 20–26. The wars are campaigns fought and won by God Himself, using the Israelites as His agents. In fighting these wars, Israel must act in a prescribed manner, observing stipulations of holy conduct. Ahab is willing to accept divine victory, but he has violated the rules for the holy war by making a treaty with Ben-hadad and yoking Israel to a foreign power (Deut. 7:1–6; 20:16–18).

**your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.** Even though each person is responsible for his conduct before God, the actions of individuals inevitably affect the lives of others for good or ill.

About twenty-four miles (39 km) north of Samaria. It is a strategic site located next to a major international route though the Jezreel Valley. Ahab maintains a palace here in addition to one in the capital (18:45). Excavations at Tel Jezreel have revealed an acropolis built during the ninth century B.C.. and constructed of dressed masonry similar to that used at Samaria and elsewhere.

In the Canaanite nations of Ahab’s day, a king can seize property and personal belongings at his pleasure, because in theory all the property is owned by the royal family and only entrusted to their subjects. In Israel, God owns the land (Ex. 19:3–8; Lev. 25:23), and the people hold it as His stewards (Num. 14:8; 35:34; Deut. 1:8). The powers of an Israelite monarch are limited, in contrast to the powers of a Canaanite king (Deut. 17:14–20; 1 Sam. 8:9–19; 10:25). When Ahab wants his neighbor’s vineyard, his thought is to negotiate a purchase (cf. 16:24).

Naboth’s reaction is quick because his land is a sacred inheritance from the Lord. When the land was distributed after the conquest (Josh. 13–21), each family received an inheritance as a divine gift and a trust. Since Naboth’s vineyard is his portion of his family’s inheritance, to sell it would mean cutting off his descendants (Lev. 25:23; Num. 27:1–11; 36:1–12). Ahab’s demand disregards God’s law.

Jezebel’s father is king in Sidon (16:31), and her understanding of the rights of a ruler are certainly different from what the law of God prescribes (Deut. 17:14–20). Kings of the nations surrounding Israel can simply seize property for their own benefit.

verse_quote: she wrote letters ... to the elders and the leaders.
note: Jezebel uses the royal power to have Naboth falsely accused and executed.

Jezebel, with Ahab’s complicity, fosters apprehensiveness among the town’s inhabitants because fasting is a characteristic response to a crisis or major transgression (Judg. 20:26; 1 Sam. 7:5, 6; 2 Chr. 20:3; Jon. 3:5, 7–9). The call for a fast will also bring all the people together as witnesses to the sham court proceedings.

The law of Israel stipulates that at least two witnesses are required to convict a person of a capital offense (Num. 35:30; Deut. 17:5, 6; 19:15).

**cursed God and the king.** The penalty for cursing God is death (Ex. 22:28; Lev. 24:10–16).
In accordance with the law, the murderers avoid ritual impurity (Lev. 24:14; Num. 15:35, 36). In 2 Kin. 9:26, Naboth’s sons are also killed, eliminating any possible heirs.
A sense of ironic justice: Ahab’s blood will be licked up by dogs in the same place where Naboth’s blood was licked up by dogs.

verse_quote: dogs ... birds of the heavens shall eat.
note: See 14:11 and note.
See 16:30–33 and notes.
The pre-Israelite inhabitants of Canaan (Gen. 15:16; Deut. 1:7; 2 Sam. 21:2).

verse_quote: tore his clothes and put sackcloth on.
note: God’s judgment, uttered through Elijah, changes Ahab’s attitude. Tearing clothes and wearing sackcloth are marks of mourning and repentance (Gen. 37:34; 2 Sam. 3:31; 2 Kin. 6:30; Lam. 2:10; Joel 1:13).

verse_quote: I will not bring the disaster in his days.
note:
God revises the punishment He gave in vv. 21–24. The penalty is not rescinded but delayed a generation due to God’s mercy.

**his son’s days.** That is, Joram (2 Kin. 9:25, 26). Though Ahab will not live to see the end of his dynasty, he and Jezebel die shameful deaths (22:37, 38; 2 Kin. 9:10, 34–37).

Israel had peace for three years after the two-year war between Syria and Israel described in 20:1–34. During this peace, Had­adezer (Ben-hadad II) of Syria, Ahab of Israel, and ten other kings formed a coalition to ward off an Assyrian invasion led by Shalmaneser III. Assyrian records report that in the major battle of this campaign fought at Qarqar, Syria, on the Orontes River (853 B.C.), Ahab contributed two hundred chariots and ten thousand soldiers. Assyria’s claim to have won a great victory seems to be an exaggeration, because the Assyrians withdrew and did not try to invade again for about four years.
On his reign, see vv. 41–50 and 2 Kin. 3:7–27.

Located about twenty-eight miles (45 km) east of the Jordan River, near a tributary to the Yarmuk River. Ramoth-gilead became Israel’s possession during the conquest (Deut. 4:43; Josh. 20:8; cf. 1 Kin. 4:13), and Ahab thinks it is time to retrieve it from the Syrians (v. 4). The town has an important strategic value, both militarily and economically, because it lies on the major international route called the “King’s Highway.” In Ahab’s day, that highway is a major thoroughfare between Egypt and Syria.

This diplomatic language signifies Jehoshaphat’s agreement to join the campaign against the Syrians. Jehoshaphat seems to be a junior partner in this coalition rather than an equal of Ahab, for Ahab tells him what to do (v. 30). Formerly, Judah was allied with the Syrians against Israel (15:16–21), so this new arrangement marks a change in the foreign policies of both Israel and Judah. At some point earlier in Ahab’s reign, he formalized his relationship with Judah by giving his daughter Athaliah in marriage to Jehoram, the son of the king of Judah (2 Kin. 8:18, 26). Athaliah is a devoted Baal worshiper, and the diplomatic marriage introduced state-sponsored Baal worship to Judah, corrupting the worship of Yahweh (2 Kin. 11).

verse_quote: Inquire first for the word of the
note: LORD**.** It is usual to consult with God or His prophets before embarking on a major campaign (1 Sam. 23:1–4; 2 Sam. 2:1; 2 Kin. 3:11; 2 Chr. 20:3–17).

The prophets whose words are recorded in the Scriptures are only a fraction of the total number of people who called themselves prophets in those times (18:19; 2 Kin. 3:13; Jer. 28). Individuals who claimed to be prophets were also common in other societies of the ancient Near East.

**they said, “Go up.”** Most of the self-designated prophets of Judah and Israel are eager to please their patrons, usually the kings, by pronouncing flatteries and agreeable messages (Jer. 28:1–4; Amos 7:10–13). These four hundred prophets may be those left over from the Mount Carmel confrontation (18:19–25).

verse_quote: Is there not here another prophet of the
note: LORD**.** Jehoshaphat is skeptical of Ahab’s prophets.

The name Micaiah means “who is like Yahweh?” He appears only in this chapter.

**he never prophesies good concerning me.** According to Jeremiah, one should be wary of prophets who prophesy too optimistically about the nation’s future (Jer. 29:8, 9).
Ahab and Jehoshaphat sit in the city at the place where judicial and municipal decisions are made (Deut. 21:19; 25:7; Ruth 4:1–12; Amos 5:10–15).

One of the prophets sought out by Ahab.

**horns of iron.** The horns symbolize power (Deut. 33:17; Zech. 1:18–21). On the symbolic actions of prophets, see note on 11:30.

A conventional oath (1:17 note).

**what the Lord** **says to me.** Even if he wants to say something else, Micaiah can only speak the word of the Lord. This confirms that he is a true prophet (Deut. 18:15–22).
Micaiah is being sarcastic and mocking Ahab and the four hundred prophets.

Micaiah depicts the defeated and leaderless armies of Israel in a state of anarchy.

**that have no shepherd.** The term “shepherd” can refer to a king (Zech. 13:7). Micaiah does not identify which shepherd is meant.

verse_quote: I will go out, and will be a lying spirit.
note: One of the celestial beings carries out God’s wishes by using the four hundred prophets as a means of reinforcing a false sense of security in Ahab (1 Sam. 16:14–16; Job 1:6–8, 12; Jer. 14:14–16; 23:16, 26; Ezek. 14:9; Gal. 1:6–9).
When the battle is over, Zedekiah will be disgraced and forced to seek refuge (cf. 20:30).
Regardless of Ahab’s will, the prophecy stands.

Ahab’s disguise indicates that he fears Micaiah’s words. It is also foolish to think that one can thwart God’s will by putting on a disguise (1 Sam. 28:8).

**your robes.** Ahab cynically has Jehoshaphat dress in royal robes, hoping that if a king has to be killed in battle (v. 17), it will be Jehoshaphat.
Neutralizing the leader of an opposing army is critical, because the opposing army might then collapse.

verse_quote: the dogs licked up his blood.
note:
This action is a partial realization of Elijah’s prophecy in 21:19 (cf. 2 Kin. 9:25, 26).

**the prostitutes washed.** Possibly a reference to sacred prostitutes from the temple of Baal.

verse_quote: the ivory house that he built.
note:
Archaeological excavations at Samaria have discovered decorative ivory inlays dating to this period. The prophet Amos criticizes such extravagance (Amos 3:15).

**cities that he built.** Archaeological excavations reveal that Samaria and Megiddo were refortified during this period.

**Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.** See note on 11:41.
On the reign of Ahaziah, see vv. 51–53; 2 Kin. 1.
If Jehoshaphat is co-regent with his father, Asa, for three years, as some scholars believe, the fourth year is 869 B.C. and refers to the beginning of his independent reign.

verse_quote: doing what was right in the sight of the
note:
LORD**.** Jehoshaphat is one of the southern kings depicted in a positive light by the author of Kings.

**the high places were not taken away.** See note on 3:2.

verse_quote: Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel.
note: Whereas the early years of the divided kingdom were characterized by intermittent warfare, the treaty between Jehoshaphat and Ahab is the start of a period of peaceful relations between Judah and Israel (cf. 2 Kin. 8:18, 26).

See 2 Kin. 3:7–27; 2 Chr. 17:11; 20.

See note on 14:24.

**Ophir.** See note on 9:28.

Ahab and Jezebel (16:29–34).

**in the way of Jeroboam.** See note on 12:30.

note: The worship of Baal, introduced and supported by Ahab and Jezebel, is perpetuated by their son (16:31 note).
